guards.rule: Planned outdoor platform elements (terrace/balcony slabs) must be built into the scene; a conservation C3 loss of a planned platform is a build-stage defect, not a reading error.
A planned outdoor platform or terrace slab that is in the build plan must be emitted as scene geometry; a missing object is a build-stage loss, not a reading or furniture issue.

When a level's outer walls do not close (walls form separate parts or a label lies in no closed face), the reading must repair the wall closure before the level is accepted; a level that cannot be closed is a reading failure, not a reason to silently drop it.
A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must not overlap; the fitter must find a non-clashing position before the run is accepted.
A bathroom or WC room must have its wet fixtures (toilet, washbasin, shower/bathtub) built and visible; a room typed bathroom with no toilet is a build-stage fit failure, not a camera or decor issue.
Two openings (doors or windows) on the same wall must not overlap; the build stage must resolve the overlap by re-placing one opening on a free span before the run is accepted.

An opening on an upper floor that opens onto nothing (no balcony, terrace, or steps) must be flagged as a reading error; the reading stage must verify that every exterior opening has a corresponding outdoor space or landing before it is built.
A balcony or terrace edge that is open over a drop must have a guard or wall behind it; the build stage must add a guard to any open edge of an outdoor space.

A light switch must be placed on the latch side of a room door, not on the door itself; the build stage must ensure that switch plates are placed on the wall adjacent to the door, not on the door leaf.

A drawn opening that the decision stage turned into a door must not overlap an existing door on the same wall; the reading must keep the opening as a passage or merge it with the door, not build a second door on top of it.
Two doors or openings that overlap on the same wall between the same two rooms are a duplicate reading; the reading must merge them into a single passage, not build two doors in the same span.

A fridge must stand on the floor, in the tall-unit column or at a run end; where it meets a counter run the run ends at it and continues past it (no worktop over the fridge). The fit stage must place the fridge clear of the counter run.
A hung washbasin must not hang over a door or opening on its wall; the fit stage must move it to a solid stretch of wall clear of the opening.
A fridge must have at least 0.50 m free in front of it for its door to open and 0.70 m to use; the fit stage must place it with its front clear of any wall or obstruction.

Every room must be reachable from outside or from a circulation space; if the reading finds no door, opening, open-plan join or stair leading to a room, the reading must add a door in the gap or correct the room's connectivity.
Every room outline must be reachable: the reading must place a door or open-plan join on its boundary; a room with no opening to a hall, stair or another room is a lost-room signal, not a valid plan.
Scene geometry checks (S5) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
A soft seat's back, back cushion and arms must rest against its seat with no gap over 5 mm; the build stage's rest plan is responsible for this.
The build's clash resolver must leave no two pieces overlapping; a residual furniture clash means the resolver failed and the level's build must be re-run.
Scene geometry checks (S1) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S2) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S4) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Scene geometry checks (S6) must pass for every level; a failure count means the build left geometry inconsistent and must be rerun.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the agent stage; if a piece is missing, the agent must re-place it.
The build stage must place every piece the final stage lists for a level; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the level's build must be re-run.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build stage must be re-run to regenerate it.
Furniture placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to re-place it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists for a level; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build for that level must be re-run.
Furniture present in the final stage but absent after the build stage is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run so the level's pieces are regenerated and re-checked.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build for that level must be re-run.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build stage must be re-run for that level.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after the build, the build must be re-run to re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build must be re-run for that level.

A piece that the final stage lists for a room must be present after the build stage; if the build drops it without a recorded reason, the build stage must be re-run so the piece is placed and the conservation check re-passes.
Boundary walls read on a level other than the ground floor (L0) are not part of the site; the reading must not record them as site items, and the building stage must not be expected to use them.

A stair room whose stair fills the room and whose only camera point is inside the stair must not be given its own interior camera; the stair is shown from the hall or landing that opens onto it, and the stair room's view is the hall's view of the stair.
A wall component without room labels that the reading records as site (not part of the building) is correctly not built; the reading's decision to record it in site is the correct handling.
A room label that lies outside the building (outside the plot) is a reading artifact, not a lost room; the reading correctly flags it and does not build it.

A washbasin must be built with a model whose name or audit identifies it as a washbasin, vanity, or bathroom fixture; a model named only as a sink (kitchen sink) is not a washbasin and must be swapped.
A washbasin must be built with a model whose name or audit identifies it as a washbasin, vanity or bathroom basin; a bare sink model is a kitchen sink and is refused for a washbasin.
A living room must contain a sofa, sofa_corner or armchair; if the model has none, the seating group is missing and must be placed.
A bedroom must contain a bed (bed_double, bed_single, bed or bed_bunk); if the model has none, the sleeping group is missing and must be placed.
A living room's seating group (sofa or armchair) is a required functional piece; if the model has none, the build stage failed to place the room's main group and must be re-run.
A bedroom's bed is a required functional piece; if the model has no bed, the build stage failed to place the room's main group and must be re-run.

A room typed living must have its seating group (sofa or armchair) built; if the reading left the room's drawn seating untyped or dropped it, the furniture stage must place the group before the run is accepted.
A room typed bedroom must have its bed built; if the reading left the drawn bed untyped or dropped it, the furniture stage must place the sleeping group before the run is accepted.
A desk read against a wall must be snapped to it; a visible gap behind a wall-backed desk is a reading placement error, not a design choice.

A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a generic table or chair but sits where a washbasin belongs must be retyped to washbasin; the room's missing wet fixture is the misread piece, not a missing one.
A bathroom's large untyped drawn element that sits where a shower or bathtub belongs must be typed to that wet fixture; an untyped piece in a wet room is a misread fixture, not a missing one.
A kitchen's untyped drawn element that sits where a fridge belongs must be typed to fridge; an untyped piece in a kitchen is a misread appliance, not a missing one.
A kitchen's untyped or mis-typed drawn element that sits where a fridge belongs must be typed to fridge; a misread piece in a kitchen is a misread appliance, not a missing one.
A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a shower but sits where a toilet belongs must be retyped to toilet; the room's missing toilet is the misread piece, not a missing one.
A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a sofa but sits where a toilet belongs must be retyped to toilet; the room's missing toilet is the misread piece, not a missing one.

A drawn piece in a bathroom whose footprint and shape match a wet fixture (bathtub or shower) must be typed as that fixture, not left untyped; an untyped piece is never built, so the room is left without its wet fixture.
A kitchen counter leg must not stop short of a door or passage; the reading stage must ensure the counter outline does not block a door's or passage's approach.
An opening of the documents must be cut through its wall; if the door ray hits a wall, the build stage must re-run to fix the geometry.

Every door and window opening read from the documents must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect that must be re-run for that level.
Every door and window opening read from the plan must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect and the level's scene must be re-run.
Every door and window opening read from the plan must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect that must be re-run for that level.

Every exterior entrance door must be reachable from the street by a continuous paved path (or terrace/flight) that lands on its threshold; a door whose landing is not connected to the site paths is an open circulation defect the architect must close.
A facade opening that is a bare gap (no door, no glass) onto the ground or a roof is not a valid opening; the architect must close it with a door, a window, or a solid wall.

Every room must be reachable from the entrance through doors and stairs; a room graph in which a large share of rooms is unreachable is a circulation defect the architect must close by adding the missing doors or stair connections.

Every level must be reachable from the entrance through a stair or lift; a level with no reachable room is a circulation defect the architect must close by adding the missing stair or lift connection.

A level that has no stair, lift or ramp connecting it to an adjacent level is not a habitable floor: the reading must flag it as a missing vertical-circulation element (or a misread level) before the build, and the build must not furnish a level that is unreachable from the entrance.
A living room must have at least one window to the outside; if the reading finds none, it must flag the missing window before the build.
An opening must not overlap a door; the reading must resolve the conflict by re-reading the wall or adjusting the opening's position.
A door must fit within its wall; if the door runs past the end of the wall, the reading must re-read the wall length or the door position.

A door whose two sides resolve to the same room outline is a reading error: the reading must split the outline at the missing wall or re-assign the door to the wall that separates two distinct rooms; a door that does not separate two rooms is not built.

A door with no room on either side is a reading error: the reading must assign the door to a wall that separates two rooms, or mark it as a shaft/void opening; a door that does not join two rooms is not built.

A door that opens onto a part of its room that no way joins to the room's main floor is a build-stage defect: the build must join that part to the main floor by a 0.80 m way before the run is accepted.
A piece that stands in front of a room's door blocks its approach; the fit stage must place pieces clear of every door's swing and approach path.
Two doors on the same wall must be placed with at least 0.10 m of wall between their frames; the build stage must space door openings so their frames never touch or run into each other at a corner.
Two door frames on the same wall must keep at least 0.10 m of clear wall between them; the build stage must re-space or re-seat the doors when their frames touch.
Two door frames that meet at a corner must not run into each other; the build stage must re-seat them so their frames do not collide.
A door frame must not run into another opening's frame at a corner; the build stage must re-seat the door so its frame does not collide with the adjacent opening.
Every freestanding stove or hob must have a cooker hood above it, sized to it, as part of the kitchen run; the build stage must place the hood when it places the stove.
A path must not run into the house; the build stage must route paths so they end at a door or landing, not at a wall.
The main entrance must be reachable from the street along the designated paths; the build stage must ensure the path network connects the street to the main entrance.
A stair's rail must not run through a wall; the build stage must build the guards as one continuous balustrade per open side, stopped under the slab and beside the floor guard of the level above.

A wall item (tv, art, holder) must not be covered by a piece standing in front of its wall; the decor stage's wall-item pass must raise the item over what stands below it, move it along its wall, or leave it out.

A wall-hung fixture (washbasin, mirror, cabinet) whose footprint overlaps a window's extent is not a clash: the window is a glazed opening, not a hole. Only an opening that drops to the floor (door, stair, shaft) is a real clash for a hung item.

A hung wall item (mirror, picture, shelf) must not be placed on a wall span where a standing piece (bookshelf, wardrobe, cabinet) occupies the same horizontal extent; the decor stage must check for standing furniture before placing a hung item.
A sofa in a WC or bathroom is a misread: the piece should be removed or retyped. The build stage must not place a sofa in a room smaller than 5 m2 unless the room type is living or bedroom.
A bathroom with a washbasin must have a mirror over it; the decor stage must complete the bathroom set.
A console table's front faces into the room, not along its long side; the recognition stage must read the front from the plan crop, not from the AI's default.
A sofa's front faces into the room, not along its long side; the recognition stage must read the front from the plan crop, not from the AI's default.
A console table's front is its long side facing the room; a front read on its short side (an AI front) is a recognition error and must be set to the long side with the most free space.
A sofa's front is its long side facing the room; a front read on its short side (an AI front) is a recognition error and must be set to the long side with the most free space.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build stage for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.
Every inside door must have a recorded leaf state; an inside door stands open by default (UL116), so the build must record the state of every inside door.
A door that a camera view sees into a room worth showing must stand open so the view is not blocked by a closed leaf (UL126); the build's door_states.revise_for_cameras must open it.

A door that a room camera looks through into a room worth showing must be left open (leaf out of the view line) by the build's door-state revision; a closed leaf in the frame is a build defect, not a camera defect.
A door a camera view looks through into a room worth showing must be left open (leaf out of the view); the build's door-state pass for cameras owns this.
Every room door gets a light switch on its latch side at 1.05 m; the build's wall-plate pass owns this.
A kitchen gets power sockets over its worktop; the build's wall-plate pass owns this.
A room's bed zone takes one light; a second light hung over the same zone is removed by the decor stage.
A room's ceiling light count follows the lumen method for its area and type; the decor stage owns this.

Every room must be lit to its lumen target: the decor stage must hang the number of ceiling lights the rule computes for the room's area and type, and a room with zero ceiling lights is a decor failure, not a taste preference.

The decor stage must hang the ceiling lights the lumen rule computes for every room it dresses; a level whose rooms all come out with zero ceiling lights means the lighting step was skipped and the stage must be re-run.
Every room must be lit to its lumen target: the decor stage must hang the computed number of ceiling lights in each room; a room with zero ceiling lights is a decor failure, not a taste preference.

Every room must be lit to its lumen-method count; the decor stage owns the ceiling-light count and the build owns the fixtures, so a room with 0 lights is a decor-stage omission, not a taste preference.
Every room must be lit to its lumen target: the decor stage must place the computed number of ceiling lights in each room; a room with zero ceiling lights is a decor failure, not a taste preference.

Every room must be lit to its lumen target: the decor stage must hang the number of ceiling lights the rule computes for the room's area and type, and a room left with zero ceiling lights is a decor failure, not a taste preference.

The decor stage's lighting pass must hang the ceiling lights the lumen rule computes for every room of a level; a level whose rooms all show zero ceiling lights is a decor-stage failure, not a per-room taste choice.
The main entrance door must be built from a statement door family (UL65), not a generic leaf; the build stage's opening-model step must assign a role-appropriate family to the entrance door.

Every drawn furniture outline must be typed by a rule or model before the build stage; an outline that no rule or model types is a reading-stage loss and must be resolved (typed, merged into a host, or marked not-furniture) before the run is accepted.

A decor piece assigned to a host must only be placed on a host that has a buildable top surface; if the host has no top, the decor must be re-hosted to a piece that does or dropped, not left un-rested.

A soft decor (cushion, throw) must rest with at least 80% of its footprint over the support and a gap under 1 cm; if no orientation satisfies both, the decor must be re-hosted or dropped, not left un-rested.
A throw or cushion may only be hosted on a piece that has a seat or arm surface; if the host lacks one, the decor must be re-hosted or dropped.
A decor piece must not penetrate its host by more than 1 cm; if the resting position causes penetration, the decor must be re-positioned or dropped.
A throw must not be penetrated by its host; if the host pokes through the cloth, the throw must be re-positioned or dropped.
A decor piece must not be placed where another already-built decor piece covers the host's top; if the spot is occupied, the decor must be re-positioned or dropped.

When two drawn outlines share a centre and one lies mostly inside the other, the inner outline is a detail of the outer piece, not a separate piece; the reading stage must merge them and keep the stronger-typed outline.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece; the reading stage must merge them unless an AI pass or rule explicitly types the inner outline as its own piece.
A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece of the same type is a duplicate of that piece, not a second piece; the reading must drop it as a duplicate, not leave it untyped.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside a larger fixture of a different type is a detail of that fixture (a bowl, a front, a panel), not a piece of its own; the reading must drop it as a detail, not leave it untyped.
A camera the baseline set (set 1) defines must be carried through every stage; if a stage drops it without a recorded reason, the cameras stage must be re-run to restore it.
A label that names a sub-zone of a larger room (an entry/antre inside a living room) is a zone of that room, not a room of its own; the reading must keep it as a zone label, not split the room.
A reading warning that records the evidence for a layer choice (which layer was chosen and why) is a record, not a lost element; it is not a finding.

A drawn outline that is a rug or group outline (drawn inside or around a seating group) is a decor element, not a furniture piece; the decor stage lays rugs under the groups, so the reading must not leave it as a lost piece.

A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a drawing mark (a tap, a valve, a threshold or shelf line), not a piece; the reading must drop it as a mark, not leave it as a lost piece.

A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m both ways that fits no furniture type is a drawing mark (a tap, a valve, a threshold or shelf line), not a piece; the reading must drop it as a mark, not leave it as a lost piece.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece (e.g., a lamp base, a sink bowl) and must not be built as an independent piece.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and must not be built as an independent piece.
A symbol that is consistently identified as non-furniture in both reading passes is an architectural obstacle or mark, not a piece, and must not be built.
A drawn outline with a dimension thinner than 0.2 m is a line or mark (e.g., threshold, shelf edge), not a furniture piece, and must not be built.
A large drawn outline that surrounds one or more other pieces is a rug or zone boundary, not a furniture piece, and must not be built as a solid object.
A drawn outline with a dimension thinner than 0.2 m is a line or mark, not a furniture piece, and must not be built.
A drawn outline that is contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and must not be built as an independent piece.
If a registered transform is rotated or skewed in a way that does not align with the level's walls, the level should keep its own frame to ensure correct geometry.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on one side is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m on both sides is a detail line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn outline that sits 60% or more inside an already-typed piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded.
A drawn outline that encloses one or more pieces is a rug or zone outline, not a piece; rugs are laid by the decor rules, not built as furniture.
A wall-layer selection note in the reading ledger is a decision record, not a lost element; it does not require a build fix.
A drawn outline that sits inside a larger piece is a cushion, pillow or detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a detail line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded from the build.
When a registered transform's scale does not match the drawing unit, the level keeps its own frame (origin at its walls); this is a correct fallback, not a loss.

When the AI passes name a bathtub for a bathroom room whose set misses a shower|bathtub, and the drawn outline's long side is between 1.4 m and 2.6 m, the reading must accept it as a bathtub even if it exceeds the standard size range, because the AI's naming is a strong signal and the room's set requires it.

When the AI passes name a bathtub for a bathroom room whose set misses a shower|bathtub, and the drawn outline's long side is between 1.4 m and 2.6 m, the reading must accept it as a bathtub even if it exceeds the standard size range.
When walls are drawn as face lines on specific layers and columns join the walls, the reading notes the layer structure and the unmodelled column area; this is a reading note, not a loss.
When a registered transform is rotated or skewed, the level keeps its own frame (origin at its walls); this is a correct fallback, not a loss.
Site boundary walls are read once on the ground floor; identical perimeter walls repeated in upper-level plans are not new site elements and their non-use is expected, not a loss.
Decor symbols read outside the building's ground-floor walls are site elements; their non-use in the interior build is expected and not a loss.
Floor marks that are stair landings within a shaft are not building levels; their non-use as level definitions is expected.
A drawn piece that is >=60% inside an existing piece on another level is a repeat of the same element in the drawing, not a new piece; its non-build is expected.
A drawn piece that is >=60% inside an existing piece on the same level is a part of that piece, not a new piece; its non-build is expected.
A drawn mark that is 60% or more inside an already-built piece of the same type is a segment of that piece, not a separate lost piece; the reading must not flag it as a duplicate.
The reading's layer-selection rationale is an informational log, not a lost element; it must not be reported as a finding.
A drawn outline that encloses a seating group and is flagged as a rug or zone outline is decor, not a furniture piece; it is correctly not built as a piece.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece; it is correctly not built.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line (threshold, valve, shelf edge), not a furniture piece, and must be excluded from the build.
An outline drawn inside another piece (a cushion, pillow or detail) is part of that piece, not a piece of its own.
A large outline enclosing a seating group is a rug or zone outline, handled by the decor rules, not a furniture piece.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line, not a furniture piece.
A large outline enclosing a group is a rug or zone outline, handled by the decor rules.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m both ways is a line, not a furniture piece.
An outline drawn mostly inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a piece of its own.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line (threshold, shelf, valve), not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A shape drawn inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A large outline enclosing other pieces is a rug or zone outline, not a piece; rugs are added by the decor stage, not the build.
A symbol both reading passes classify as not_furniture is an obstacle or mark, not a piece, and must not be built.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m on both sides is a line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
The bed-pillow front rule applies only to beds; for other piece types the front is inferred from the piece's own geometry, not from pillow shapes.
null

A drawn outline that encloses a seating group and is thinner than 0.2 m on its border, or matches a rug aspect ratio, is a zone/rug outline, not a furniture piece; the decor stage places the rug, the build stage does not.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on its narrowest side is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf edge), not a furniture piece; the reading must classify it as a mark, not a piece.

When a layer contains only LINE entities (no hatches, text, or blocks) and none of its geometry is used by the model, the reading must either map it to a model element (e.g., ceiling grid, partition) or explicitly record it as annotation/annotation-only with a reason, so it does not appear as an unexplained unused layer.
A piece typed as ottoman in a hall room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a hall-appropriate type (console_table, bench, or shoe_cabinet) based on its size and position.
A piece typed as washbasin in a hall room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a hall-appropriate type (console_table, sideboard, or shoe_cabinet) based on its size and position.
A piece typed as shower in a WC room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a WC-appropriate type (toilet, washbasin) based on its size and position.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate. This must be checked for every level, not just the first.
An exterior door that lands on the lawn must have a path, terrace, or steps leading from its landing to the site; the site stage must add the connection.

Elevation checks against plans require a north arrow to orient the building; if the north arrow is missing from the drawing, the reading must flag it as a missing datum and the elevations cannot be verified.

An elevation whose openings cannot be checked against the plans for lack of a north arrow is a missing reference datum, not a model defect; it is held for the architect to supply the orientation, not fixed in the build.

The main entrance door must be taller and wider than the interior doors it serves; the build's door-sizing step must apply the entrance's product size (UL117) rather than leaving it at the interior door's dimensions.

A room typed as a kitchen (or carrying a kitchen zone) must always receive a counter run, even a compact one; the build must not leave a kitchen zone empty when no candidate position fits, but must place a compact run.
A hall/entry room must receive its entrance group (console or lit niche); the decor stage must not leave a hall empty when no candidate position fits, but must place a compact entrance piece.
A WC room must always receive its wc_set (toilet and washbasin); the build must not leave a WC empty when no candidate position fits, but must place a compact set.
A bathroom must always receive its bathroom_set (wet fixtures); the build must not leave a bathroom empty when no candidate position fits, but must place a compact set.
When no library model fits an opening's size, the build may fall back to a parametric opening in the style's finish; this is an acceptable library gap, not a defect to fix.
When no library model fits an inside door's size, the build may fall back to a parametric door in the style's finish; this is an acceptable library gap, not a defect to fix.
When no library model of the house's door family fits the drawn opening, a parametric door in the style's finish is the correct build; the library gap is recorded, not a defect.
When the only library model for an opening would require non-uniform stretching to fit, a parametric opening is the correct build; the library gap is recorded, not a defect.

A piece built below the library level (parametric mesh) when a library model fits its size and style must be swapped to the library model; the fit stage must prefer library models over parametric meshes when one is available.
A bathroom tall_cabinet must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A bathroom toilet must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A wc toilet must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A living chaise must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A living tv_unit must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A bedroom nightstand must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A bedroom desk must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A living sofa must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.
A living table_coffee must be a finished library model, not the parametric mesh; the fit stage must pick a library asset that matches the room's palette.

A kitchen_counter piece with a footprint under 0.10 m on a side is a misread sliver, not a real counter; the reading stage must drop it or merge it into the adjacent counter run, and the fit stage must not build a parametric mesh for a sliver.

The fit stage must prefer a library model over the parametric family whenever a library model exists for the piece's type and its footprint fits the drawn size; the parametric mesh is a fallback only when no library model matches, so a piece is never built below the library level while a suitable model is available.

A piece fitted to a parametric mesh when a library model of the same footprint and style family is available is a fit-stage defect: the fitter must take the library model, not the parametric fallback.
A kitchen worktop with free length must carry the family's styling sets (cookware, jars, boards, bottles) beyond the small appliances; an empty worktop is a decor-stage omission.
A kitchen worktop with free length must carry the family's styling sets (cookware, jars, boards, bottles) beyond the small appliances; an under-styled worktop is a decor-stage omission.
Every room door must have a light switch on its latch side; a door without one while the room's other door has one is a build-stage omission.
A wall cabinet's joints must align with the base units' joints under it; a misaligned joint is a build-stage defect in the kitchen run.
A room's ceiling light count must match the lumen method for its area and style; a count below the computed value is a decor-stage omission.
A living room must have a TV on a wall facing the seating 1.5-4 m away, clear of windows and doors; a living room with no valid TV place is a layout-stage defect.
A bedroom must have a TV on a wall facing the bed 1.5-4 m away, clear of windows and doors; a bedroom with no valid TV place is a layout-stage defect.
A furnished living room must be at least 25 % furnished; a living room under 25 % is a decor-stage omission.
A bathroom must have storage (a tall cabinet or similar) alongside its fixtures; a bathroom with no storage is a layout-stage omission.
A bathroom's program includes a storage element (tall cabinet or shelf); the layout stage must place it with the wet fixtures, not leave the fixtures standing alone.
A wood floor in a living or bedroom must be laid in a patterned parquet (herringbone or chevron), not plain planks, to meet the professional finish bar.
A bedroom's wood floor must be laid in a herringbone or chevron parquet pattern, not plain planks, to meet the professional finish bar.
Every washbasin in a bathroom or WC must have a mirror above it; the decor stage's bath dressing is responsible for placing the family's mirror.
A hall or entry room must carry a console table or a lit wall niche as its defining piece; the decor stage's room_details is responsible for it.
A hall smaller than about 1.5 m² is a passage stub: the console/niche detail (H1, H4) is waived because no wall length or floor area can hold the piece.
A bed's bedding set must include the throw pair across its foot; if the bedding plan omits it, the decor stage must re-run to dress the bed.
A kitchen worktop with free length must carry the family's styling sets (cookware, jars, boards, bottles); if the worktop is bare, the decor stage must re-run to place them.

Every opening the reading stage records (doors, windows, openings) must be carried into the built geometry; the build stage must not drop a recorded opening, and a conservation check that finds a recorded opening missing from the final stage is a build-stage defect to be re-run.

An opening that the reading stage leaves in the unverified list (no confirmed drawing evidence) is not a loss when the build stage omits it; only openings with confirmed evidence are required in the model.

A door confirmed by the reading stage (named in openings with evidence) must be cut into its wall by the build stage; a confirmed opening that is absent from the built geometry is a build-stage defect that requires a re-run of the build for that level.

When the reading stage rejects a window in architect_defaults because it is adjacent to a door's side misread as a window, the build stage is correct to omit it; the fix belongs to the reading stage correcting the door-side misread, not to the build stage building a rejected window.
A confirmed opening (named in openings with evidence) must be present in the built geometry; if the build stage drops it, the build for that level must be re-run.

A typed functional piece (kitchen counter, stove, fridge, cabinet) that the documents show must be built and visible; if the build stage drops it, the level's build must be re-run so the piece is placed and the scene re-checked.

When a drawn kitchen run is split into multiple counter segments, the build stage merges them into one built counter; the per-segment piece ids are consumed by the merge and their disappearance is expected, not a loss.

A drawn symbol that the reading stage leaves unverified and the build stage does not promote is a reading artifact; its absence from the built model is expected and is not a loss of a required element.
An untyped (unknown) drawn mark that the build stage cannot resolve to a furniture type is dropped, not a lost element; only typed pieces the documents show are conservation losses.
A model the user has rejected is excluded from the asset list and must not be built; its absence is a correct exclusion, not a conservation loss.
A piece dropped by the build stage to resolve a placement conflict is not a conservation loss when the room's functional group is already satisfied by another piece of the same type.

A drawn mark that is untyped and conflicts with the room's built geometry is dropped by the build stage; its absence from the final stage is not a conservation loss unless the documents show it is a required built element.
A drawn mark that is untyped and unverified by the build stage is not a required element; its absence from the final stage is not a conservation loss.

A drawn kitchen fixture (stove, fridge, counter) that conflicts with built geometry must be re-placed by the build stage to a valid spot, not dropped; a conflict on a required fixture is a build defect.
A drawn furniture piece that conflicts with built geometry must be re-placed by the build stage to a valid spot, not dropped; a conflict on a required piece is a build defect.
A drawn wardrobe that is unverified by the build stage must be verified and built; an unverified required bedroom piece is a build defect.
A drawn furniture piece that blocks a window or door approach must be re-placed by the build stage clear of the approach, not dropped; a piece that blocks a passage is a build defect.
A drawn kitchen fixture (fridge, stove, counter) listed in a room's zone must be built by the build stage; a listed required fixture that is dropped is a build defect.
A drawn kitchen fixture (fridge, stove, counter) flagged by a project rule must be built by the build stage; a flagged required fixture that is dropped is a build defect.
A piece excluded by an explicit user rejection recorded in the run is a deliberate removal, not a conservation loss; the build stage is correct to leave it unbuilt.

A piece dropped by the build stage because of a placement conflict must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; a conflict is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn piece.

A wet fixture (washbasin) dropped by the build stage because of a placement conflict must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; a conflict is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.

A wet fixture (shower) dropped by the build stage because of a placement conflict must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; a conflict is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.

A wet fixture (toilet) dropped by the build stage because of a placement conflict must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; a conflict is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.

A wet fixture (washbasin) left unverified and dropped by the build stage must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; an unverified fixture is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.

A kitchen counter left unverified and dropped by the build stage must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; an unverified fixture is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.

A wet fixture (washbasin) dropped by the build stage (decor_dropped) must be re-placed by the build stage, not silently removed; a dropped fixture is a placement problem to solve, not a reason to delete a drawn fixture.
A piece that blocks the only passage of a room (leaving less than 0.60 m free) must be dropped by the build stage rather than kept; the loss is correct, not a conservation failure.
A drawn piece whose front the reading cannot resolve (AI front on the wrong side) may be dropped by the build stage; the loss is a reading failure to fix upstream, not a conservation failure.
A wc_set whose anchor is retyped by code must be completed with its missing members (washbasin, toilet) by the build stage; a set that misses a member is a build failure, not a reading one.
A piece named only in a conflict record (no drawn anchor, no room-program requirement) may be dropped by the build stage; the loss is a good reason, not a conservation failure.

When the reading identifies several drawn blocks as the same physical fixture (same strokes, same footprint across levels), the build stage keeps one instance and drops the rest; the loss is correct deduplication, not a conservation failure.
A drawn symbol that the reading could not type or verify (unverified record) may be dropped by the build stage; the loss is a good reason, not a conservation failure.
A bathroom or shower room whose drawn set includes a shower must have that shower built by the build stage; dropping it leaves the room's wet function missing, which is a build failure.

When the code types a fixture from its footprint at the same plan position as an instance on another level, the build stage keeps one instance and drops the rest; the loss is correct deduplication, not a conservation failure.

When a drawn kitchen counter is consolidated into the room's built kitchen run, the individual drawn piece ids are not carried into the final scene; the conservation check must treat the built run as satisfying the drawn counter, not flag each absorbed segment as lost.
An untyped drawn symbol (type 'unknown') that the build stage does not construct is not a conservation loss; the check must only flag typed functional pieces that are missing from the built set.
An untyped drawn mark that the build stage cannot place is dropped, not a lost room element; only typed functional pieces are conserved.
A typed functional piece (sofa) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (console_table) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (armchair) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (table_coffee) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (ottoman) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (stove) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A typed functional piece (floor_lamp) that the build stage drops from a room's furnished set is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A piece the final stage placed that the build stage dropped for a conflict must be re-placed by the build stage at a non-clashing position, not silently removed.

When the same drawn block (identical strokes and footprint within tolerance) appears on stacked levels, the build stage may merge it into one shared element; the per-level instance ids are not separate drawn elements and their absence from a level's final list is not a conservation loss.

A drawn fixture that is named in a conflict record and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is re-placed and the conflict resolved, not silently dropped.

A drawn furniture piece named in a conflict record and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is re-placed and the conflict resolved, not silently dropped.
A drawn element left unverified and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is verified and placed, not silently dropped.

A drawn element named in a conflict record and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is re-placed and the conflict resolved, not silently dropped.

A drawn fixture named in a conflict record and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is re-placed and the conflict resolved, not silently dropped.
A drawn fixture typed by code and dropped by the build stage is a build-stage loss: the build stage must re-run for that level so the element is re-placed, not silently dropped.
not_a_problem

A drawn kitchen counter that is assigned to a room zone must be built and visible; if the build stage drops a typed, zone-assigned piece, the build stage must be re-run so the piece is regenerated and re-checked.

prevention.what: the model makes no sense to a visitor (a door into the air, a basin at knee height, stairs running into each other, a railing across a door)

rules_proposed.rule: Two openings (doors or windows) on the same wall must not overlap; the build stage must resolve the overlap by re-placing one opening on a free span before the run is accepted.

An opening on an upper floor that opens onto nothing (no balcony, terrace, or steps) must be flagged as a reading error; the reading stage must verify that every exterior opening has a corresponding outdoor space or landing before it is built.
A balcony or terrace edge that is open over a drop must have a guard or wall behind it; the build stage must add a guard to any open edge of an outdoor space.

A light switch must be placed on the latch side of a room door, not on the door itself; the build stage must ensure that switch plates are placed on the wall adjacent to the door, not on the door leaf.

A drawn opening that the decision stage turned into a door must not overlap an existing door on the same wall; the reading must keep the opening as a passage or merge it with the door, not build a second door on top of it.
Two doors or openings that overlap on the same wall between the same two rooms are a duplicate reading; the reading must merge them into a single passage, not build two doors in the same span.

A fridge must stand on the floor, in the tall-unit column or at a run end; where it meets a counter run the run ends at it and continues past it (no worktop over the fridge). The fit stage must place the fridge clear of the counter run.
A hung washbasin must not hang over a door or opening on its wall; the fit stage must move it to a solid stretch of wall clear of the opening.
A fridge must have at least 0.50 m free in front of it for its door to open and 0.70 m to use; the fit stage must place it with its front clear of any wall or obstruction.

Every room must be reachable from outside or from a circulation space; if the reading finds no door, opening, open-plan join or stair leading to a room, the reading must add a door in the gap or correct the room's connectivity.
Every room outline must be reachable: the reading must place a door or open-plan join on its boundary; a room with no opening to a hall, stair or another room is a lost-room signal, not a valid plan.
An opening of the documents must be cut through its wall; if the door ray hits a wall, the build stage must re-run to fix the geometry.

Every door and window opening read from the documents must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect that must be re-run for that level.
Every door and window opening read from the plan must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect and the level's scene must be re-run.
Every door and window opening read from the plan must be cut through its host wall in the build; an opening whose ray still hits the wall is a build-stage defect that must be re-run for that level.

Every exterior entrance door must be reachable from the street by a continuous paved path (or terrace/flight) that lands on its threshold; a door whose landing is not connected to the site paths is an open circulation defect the architect must close.
A facade opening that is a bare gap (no door, no glass) onto the ground or a roof is not a valid opening; the architect must close it with a door, a window, or a solid wall.

Every room must be reachable from the entrance through doors and stairs; a room graph in which a large share of rooms is unreachable is a circulation defect the architect must close by adding the missing doors or stair connections.

Every level must be reachable from the entrance through a stair or lift; a level with no reachable room is a circulation defect the architect must close by adding the missing stair or lift connection.

A level that has no stair, lift or ramp connecting it to an adjacent level is not a habitable floor: the reading must flag it as a missing vertical-circulation element (or a misread level) before the build, and the build must not furnish a level that is unreachable from the entrance.
A living room must have at least one window to the outside; if the reading finds none, it must flag the missing window before the build.
An opening must not overlap a door; the reading must resolve the conflict by re-reading the wall or adjusting the opening's position.
A door must fit within its wall; if the door runs past the end of the wall, the reading must re-read the wall length or the door position.

A door whose two sides resolve to the same room outline is a reading error: the reading must split the outline at the missing wall or re-assign the door to the wall that separates two distinct rooms; a door that does not separate two rooms is not built.

A door with no room on either side is a reading error: the reading must assign the door to a wall that separates two rooms, or mark it as a shaft/void opening; a door that does not join two rooms is not built.

A door that opens onto a part of its room that no way joins to the room's main floor is a build-stage defect: the build must join that part to the main floor by a 0.80 m way before the run is accepted.
A piece that stands in front of a room's door blocks its approach; the fit stage must place pieces clear of every door's swing and approach path.
Two doors on the same wall must be placed with at least 0.10 m of wall between their frames; the build stage must space door openings so their frames never touch or run into each other at a corner.
Two door frames on the same wall must keep at least 0.10 m of clear wall between them; the build stage must re-space or re-seat the doors when their frames touch.
Two door frames that meet at a corner must not run into each other; the build stage must re-seat them so their frames do not collide.
A door frame must not run into another opening's frame at a corner; the build stage must re-seat the door so its frame does not collide with the adjacent opening.
Every freestanding stove or hob must have a cooker hood above it, sized to it, as part of the kitchen run; the build stage must place the hood when it places the stove.
A path must not run into the house; the build stage must route paths so they end at a door or landing, not at a wall.
The main entrance must be reachable from the street along the designated paths; the build stage must ensure the path network connects the street to the main entrance.
A stair's rail must not run through a wall; the build stage must build the guards as one continuous balustrade per open side, stopped under the slab and beside the floor guard of the level above.

A wall item (tv, art, holder) must not be covered by a piece standing in front of its wall; the decor stage's wall-item pass must raise the item over what stands below it, move it along its wall, or leave it out.

A wall-hung fixture (washbasin, mirror, cabinet) whose footprint overlaps a window's extent is not a clash: the window is a glazed opening, not a hole. Only an opening that drops to the floor (door, stair, shaft) is a real clash for a hung item.

A hung wall item (mirror, picture, shelf) must not be placed on a wall span where a standing piece (bookshelf, wardrobe, cabinet) occupies the same horizontal extent; the decor stage must check for standing furniture before placing a hung item.
A sofa in a WC or bathroom is a misread: the piece should be removed or retyped. The build stage must not place a sofa in a room smaller than 5 m2 unless the room type is living or bedroom.
A bathroom with a washbasin must have a mirror over it; the decor stage must complete the bathroom set.
An exterior door that lands on the lawn must have a path, terrace, or steps leading from its landing to the site; the site stage must add the connection.

rules_proposed.rule: A room's listed functional pieces (stove, fridge, cabinets) must be built and visible; if the render shows an empty shell, the build stage failed to place them.
A bathroom's wet fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) must not overlap; the fitter must find a non-clashing position before the run is accepted.
A bathroom or WC room must have its wet fixtures (toilet, washbasin, shower/bathtub) built and visible; a room typed bathroom with no toilet is a build-stage fit failure, not a camera or decor issue.

A washbasin must be built with a model whose name or audit identifies it as a washbasin, vanity, or bathroom fixture; a model named only as a sink (kitchen sink) is not a washbasin and must be swapped.
A washbasin must be built with a model whose name or audit identifies it as a washbasin, vanity or bathroom basin; a bare sink model is a kitchen sink and is refused for a washbasin.
A living room must contain a sofa, sofa_corner or armchair; if the model has none, the seating group is missing and must be placed.
A bedroom must contain a bed (bed_double, bed_single, bed or bed_bunk); if the model has none, the sleeping group is missing and must be placed.
A living room's seating group (sofa or armchair) is a required functional piece; if the model has none, the build stage failed to place the room's main group and must be re-run.
A bedroom's bed is a required functional piece; if the model has no bed, the build stage failed to place the room's main group and must be re-run.

A room typed living must have its seating group (sofa or armchair) built; if the reading left the room's drawn seating untyped or dropped it, the furniture stage must place the group before the run is accepted.
A room typed bedroom must have its bed built; if the reading left the drawn bed untyped or dropped it, the furniture stage must place the sleeping group before the run is accepted.
A desk read against a wall must be snapped to it; a visible gap behind a wall-backed desk is a reading placement error, not a design choice.

A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a generic table or chair but sits where a washbasin belongs must be retyped to washbasin; the room's missing wet fixture is the misread piece, not a missing one.
A bathroom's large untyped drawn element that sits where a shower or bathtub belongs must be typed to that wet fixture; an untyped piece in a wet room is a misread fixture, not a missing one.
A kitchen's untyped drawn element that sits where a fridge belongs must be typed to fridge; an untyped piece in a kitchen is a misread appliance, not a missing one.
A kitchen's untyped or mis-typed drawn element that sits where a fridge belongs must be typed to fridge; a misread piece in a kitchen is a misread appliance, not a missing one.
A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a shower but sits where a toilet belongs must be retyped to toilet; the room's missing toilet is the misread piece, not a missing one.
A wc room's drawn fixture that is typed as a sofa but sits where a toilet belongs must be retyped to toilet; the room's missing toilet is the misread piece, not a missing one.

A drawn piece in a bathroom whose footprint and shape match a wet fixture (bathtub or shower) must be typed as that fixture, not left untyped; an untyped piece is never built, so the room is left without its wet fixture.
A kitchen counter leg must not stop short of a door or passage; the reading stage must ensure the counter outline does not block a door's or passage's approach.
A piece typed as ottoman in a hall room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a hall-appropriate type (console_table, bench, or shoe_cabinet) based on its size and position.
A piece typed as washbasin in a hall room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a hall-appropriate type (console_table, sideboard, or shoe_cabinet) based on its size and position.
A piece typed as shower in a WC room is a misread; the reading must retype it to a WC-appropriate type (toilet, washbasin) based on its size and position.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate.

When one room outline carries the labels of two or more rooms, the reading must split it at the missing wall before room assignment; a label with no matching room outline is a lost-room signal, not a duplicate. This must be checked for every level, not just the first.

rules_proposed.rule: Planned outdoor platform elements (terrace/balcony slabs) must be built into the scene; a conservation C3 loss of a planned platform is a build-stage defect, not a reading error.
A planned outdoor platform or terrace slab that is in the build plan must be emitted as scene geometry; a missing object is a build-stage loss, not a reading or furniture issue.

When a level's outer walls do not close (walls form separate parts or a label lies in no closed face), the reading must repair the wall closure before the level is accepted; a level that cannot be closed is a reading failure, not a reason to silently drop it.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the agent stage; if a piece is missing, the agent must re-place it.
The build stage must place every piece the final stage lists for a level; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the level's build must be re-run.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build stage must be re-run to regenerate it.
Furniture placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to re-place it.

The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists for a level; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build for that level must be re-run.
Furniture present in the final stage but absent after the build stage is a build-stage loss; the build stage must be re-run so the level's pieces are regenerated and re-checked.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after build, the build stage must be re-run to re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build for that level must be re-run.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build stage must be re-run for that level.
Pieces placed by the decor stage must be preserved by the build stage; if a piece is missing after the build, the build must be re-run to re-place it.
The build stage must preserve every piece the final stage lists; a piece present in the final stage but absent after build is a build-stage loss and the build must be re-run for that level.

A piece that the final stage lists for a room must be present after the build stage; if the build drops it without a recorded reason, the build stage must be re-run so the piece is placed and the conservation check re-passes.
Boundary walls read on a level other than the ground floor (L0) are not part of the site; the reading must not record them as site items, and the building stage must not be expected to use them.

A stair room whose stair fills the room and whose only camera point is inside the stair must not be given its own interior camera; the stair is shown from the hall or landing that opens onto it, and the stair room's view is the hall's view of the stair.
A wall component without room labels that the reading records as site (not part of the building) is correctly not built; the reading's decision to record it in site is the correct handling.
A room label that lies outside the building (outside the plot) is a reading artifact, not a lost room; the reading correctly flags it and does not build it.

When two drawn outlines share a centre and one lies mostly inside the other, the inner outline is a detail of the outer piece, not a separate piece; the reading stage must merge them and keep the stronger-typed outline.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece; the reading stage must merge them unless an AI pass or rule explicitly types the inner outline as its own piece.
A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside another piece of the same type is a duplicate of that piece, not a second piece; the reading must drop it as a duplicate, not leave it untyped.

A drawn piece that is 60% or more inside a larger fixture of a different type is a detail of that fixture (a bowl, a front, a panel), not a piece of its own; the reading must drop it as a detail, not leave it untyped.
A camera the baseline set (set 1) defines must be carried through every stage; if a stage drops it without a recorded reason, the cameras stage must be re-run to restore it.
A label that names a sub-zone of a larger room (an entry/antre inside a living room) is a zone of that room, not a room of its own; the reading must keep it as a zone label, not split the room.
A reading warning that records the evidence for a layer choice (which layer was chosen and why) is a record, not a lost element; it is not a finding.

A drawn outline that is a rug or group outline (drawn inside or around a seating group) is a decor element, not a furniture piece; the decor stage lays rugs under the groups, so the reading must not leave it as a lost piece.

A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a drawing mark (a tap, a valve, a threshold or shelf line), not a piece; the reading must drop it as a mark, not leave it as a lost piece.

A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m both ways that fits no furniture type is a drawing mark (a tap, a valve, a threshold or shelf line), not a piece; the reading must drop it as a mark, not leave it as a lost piece.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece (e.g., a lamp base, a sink bowl) and must not be built as an independent piece.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and must not be built as an independent piece.
A symbol that is consistently identified as non-furniture in both reading passes is an architectural obstacle or mark, not a piece, and must not be built.
A drawn outline with a dimension thinner than 0.2 m is a line or mark (e.g., threshold, shelf edge), not a furniture piece, and must not be built.
A large drawn outline that surrounds one or more other pieces is a rug or zone boundary, not a furniture piece, and must not be built as a solid object.
A drawn outline with a dimension thinner than 0.2 m is a line or mark, not a furniture piece, and must not be built.
A drawn outline that is contained within another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece and must not be built as an independent piece.
If a registered transform is rotated or skewed in a way that does not align with the level's walls, the level should keep its own frame to ensure correct geometry.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on one side is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m on both sides is a detail line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn outline that sits 60% or more inside an already-typed piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded.
A drawn outline that encloses one or more pieces is a rug or zone outline, not a piece; rugs are laid by the decor rules, not built as furniture.
A wall-layer selection note in the reading ledger is a decision record, not a lost element; it does not require a build fix.
A drawn outline that sits inside a larger piece is a cushion, pillow or detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a detail line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the furniture build.
A drawn outline that is 60% or more inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded from the build.
When a registered transform's scale does not match the drawing unit, the level keeps its own frame (origin at its walls); this is a correct fallback, not a loss.

When the AI passes name a bathtub for a bathroom room whose set misses a shower|bathtub, and the drawn outline's long side is between 1.4 m and 2.6 m, the reading must accept it as a bathtub even if it exceeds the standard size range, because the AI's naming is a strong signal and the room's set requires it.

When the AI passes name a bathtub for a bathroom room whose set misses a shower|bathtub, and the drawn outline's long side is between 1.4 m and 2.6 m, the reading must accept it as a bathtub even if it exceeds the standard size range.
When walls are drawn as face lines on specific layers and columns join the walls, the reading notes the layer structure and the unmodelled column area; this is a reading note, not a loss.
When a registered transform is rotated or skewed, the level keeps its own frame (origin at its walls); this is a correct fallback, not a loss.
Site boundary walls are read once on the ground floor; identical perimeter walls repeated in upper-level plans are not new site elements and their non-use is expected, not a loss.
Decor symbols read outside the building's ground-floor walls are site elements; their non-use in the interior build is expected and not a loss.
Floor marks that are stair landings within a shaft are not building levels; their non-use as level definitions is expected.
A drawn piece that is >=60% inside an existing piece on another level is a repeat of the same element in the drawing, not a new piece; its non-build is expected.
A drawn piece that is >=60% inside an existing piece on the same level is a part of that piece, not a new piece; its non-build is expected.
A drawn mark that is 60% or more inside an already-built piece of the same type is a segment of that piece, not a separate lost piece; the reading must not flag it as a duplicate.
The reading's layer-selection rationale is an informational log, not a lost element; it must not be reported as a finding.
A drawn outline that encloses a seating group and is flagged as a rug or zone outline is decor, not a furniture piece; it is correctly not built as a piece.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m that fits no furniture type is a detail line (tap, valve, threshold, shelf), not a piece; it is correctly not built.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line (threshold, valve, shelf edge), not a furniture piece, and must be excluded from the build.
An outline drawn inside another piece (a cushion, pillow or detail) is part of that piece, not a piece of its own.
A large outline enclosing a seating group is a rug or zone outline, handled by the decor rules, not a furniture piece.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line, not a furniture piece.
A large outline enclosing a group is a rug or zone outline, handled by the decor rules.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m both ways is a line, not a furniture piece.
An outline drawn mostly inside another piece is a detail of that piece, not a piece of its own.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line (threshold, shelf, valve), not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A shape drawn inside another piece's footprint is a detail of that piece, not a separate piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A large outline enclosing other pieces is a rug or zone outline, not a piece; rugs are added by the decor stage, not the build.
A symbol both reading passes classify as not_furniture is an obstacle or mark, not a piece, and must not be built.
A drawn mark thinner than 0.2 m on a side is a line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
A drawn mark smaller than 0.3 m on both sides is a line, not a piece, and must be excluded from the build.
The bed-pillow front rule applies only to beds; for other piece types the front is inferred from the piece's own geometry, not from pillow shapes.
